old: Two disciplines protect the shortlist. First, do not disclose budget to anyone paid contingent on a sale closing. Disclose use case, size band, and propulsion preference; let the broker fit yachts to the use case. The budget conversation belongs with the independent adviser. Second, walk yachts with the independent adviser alongside the broker; the independent adviser is looking for things the broker is not paid to find.
new: Two habits protect the shortlist. First, keep the budget figure with the independent adviser. Brokers on both sides of a sale are usually paid from the seller’s commission, which rises with the price (chapter 3). Written disclosure tells the buyer how a broker is paid, but a budget figure shared with the broker can still become the floor of the negotiation. Give the broker the use case, size band and propulsion preference, and let them fit yachts to it. Second, walk yachts with the independent adviser alongside the broker; the adviser is looking for things the broker is not paid to find.

old: The French Commercial Exemption (FCE) eliminates VAT entirely if its conditions are met (commercial registration, full-time crew, length above 15 metres, more than 70 percent of voyages exiting French waters, less than 50 percent static charters). Spanish Inward Processing Relief suspends 21 percent VAT on refit works for non-EU flagged yachts within an 18-month admission window. Maltese leasing no longer uses a length-based table: under guidelines of 12 March 2020, VAT on the lease follows documented use inside and outside EU waters, and the European Commission closed its infringement case that October. Italy moved to a comparable effective-use test from 1 November 2020, and leasing remains available where use can be evidenced.
new: The French Commercial Exemption (FCE) eliminates VAT entirely if its conditions are met (commercial registration, full-time crew, length above 15 metres, more than 70 percent of voyages exiting French waters, less than 50 percent static charters). Maltese leasing no longer uses a length-based table: under guidelines of 12 March 2020, VAT on the lease follows documented use inside and outside EU waters, and the European Commission closed its infringement case that October. Italy moved to a comparable effective-use test from 1 November 2020, and leasing remains available where use can be evidenced. The fourth route, Spanish inward processing, concerns refit rather than purchase. A non-EU yacht refitted at a customs-site shipyard, with authorisation in place before the works begin, is exempt from the 21 percent VAT on the works, provided the procedure is followed through to the yacht’s departure from the EU. Time under inward processing does not count against the 18-month temporary admission period. Chapter 6 sets out how it works and where compliance rests.

old: A separate UK-specific jurisdictional risk sits on top of the technical choice. The 58.5-metre Royal Huisman motor yacht Phi has been detained in London since 28 March 2022 under a direction from the UK Secretary of State for Transport, issued shortly after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Her beneficial owner has not been designated under UK sanctions; the detention has outlived the Transport Secretary who issued it, multiple governments, and several legal challenges. The UK Supreme Court dismissed the owning company’s appeal on 29 July 2025, and the owner’s team has said it intends to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights. The narrow point for a buyer weighing a Red Ensign flag for a UK-domiciled hull is that the British executive has acted, and can act, on yachts whose owners do not match the public profile of a sanctioned individual; remedy through the British court system can take years (Capt. Guy Booth, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).
new: The flag does not settle every jurisdictional risk. The 58.5-metre Royal Huisman motor yacht Phi, which flew the Maltese flag, has been detained in London since 28 March 2022 under a direction from the UK Secretary of State for Transport, issued shortly after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Her beneficial owner has not been designated under UK sanctions; the detention rests on his connection with Russia, and it has outlived the Transport Secretary who issued it, several governments and several legal challenges. The UK Supreme Court dismissed the owning company’s appeal on 29 July 2025, and the owner’s team has said it intends to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights. The point for a buyer is narrow: a state can detain a yacht in its waters whose owner is not personally sanctioned, whatever flag she flies, and a challenge through the courts can take years (Capt. Guy Booth, in The Superyacht Report, Q2 2026).
reason: Phi was Malta-flagged, so the lesson is not about choosing a Red Ensign flag; the basis of detention named. Kept in ch04 (jurisdiction risk at purchase).

new.text: Two developments in 2026 bear on how the holding structure is built. On 21 May 2026 the Court of Justice of the European Union held, in joined Cases C-428/24 and C-476/24 concerning Sailing Yacht A, that assets held in a trust can be treated under EU sanctions law as owned or controlled by a sanctioned beneficiary, and that terms in the trust deed do not of themselves prevent a freeze. The case has returned to the Italian courts and the yacht remains seized. A trust above the yacht’s holding company is a succession arrangement; it does not place the yacht beyond measures aimed at the person who benefits from it. Separately, Switzerland opened a federal register of beneficial owners on 1 October 2026. It is not public, but a Swiss company, or a foreign holding company whose decisions are in practice taken in Switzerland, must file the natural persons who control it, with changes reported within a month. From the same date, Swiss lawyers, fiduciaries and multi-family offices that set up or fund a company abroad for a client carry anti-money-laundering due diligence, including questions on the source of funds where the risk warrants it.
